To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TLR2 and/or TLR4 play a critical role in host defense against mycobacterial infections, but the specific role of each receptor depends on the nature of the mycobacterial challenge.

TLR2‐ and TLR4‐deficient mice differ markedly in their susceptibility to BCG infection, that BCG growth is controlled by IFN‐γ‐dependent and IFN‐ γ‐ independent mechanisms, and that the role of IFN‐γ appears to be regulated by TLRs.
Toll‐like receptors TLR2 and 4 serve distinct roles as sensors of mycobacteria and as regulators of the host immune responses that are induced by infection with Mycobacterium.

the molecular basis of innate immunity to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
how the host immune system controls the growth of mycobacteria and the mechanisms by which the host immune response is regulated by TLRs.
the role of toll‐like receptors in the immune response against mycobacterial infections.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TLR2 and 4 have distinct roles in controlling the host immune response and bacterial growth against mycobacteria.
TLR2 and 4 have different functions in the immune response against B. Calmette‐Guérin (BCG), the live attenuated strain of M. bovis.

TLR2 is essential for the control of mycobacterial growth and the induction of IFN‐γ secretion in vivo and TLR4 is essential for the induction of cytokine secretion by BCG‐stimulated macrophages in vitro.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TLR2 and 4 have distinct functions during the host response against mycobacteria.

the TLRs are differentially involved in the host response to mycobacteria, with TLR2 being important for the induction of innate immune responses, while TLR4 is more involved in the induction of adaptive immunity.
